lessons.title: First Contact
objectives: greet someone formally and informally
say your name and ask another person’s name
recognize tu and vous as different levels of formality

teaching.explanation: French greetings are short chunks. Learn them as complete actions before analyzing grammar. Salut can be used informally; bonjour is the standard daytime greeting; bonsoir is used in the evening. Tu is the familiar singular “you”; vous is the formal singular (and also the plural) “you.”
teaching.pattern: Je m'appelle + name = My name is + name. Comment tu t'appelles ? = What is your name? (informal). Comment vous appelez-vous ? = What is your name? (formal)
teaching.culture_note: Use vous when you want to show respect or when regional/register norms are unknown; tu is common with peers and in many everyday casual settings.

examples.analysis: bonjour = hello; je m'appelle = my name is
comment = how; tu t'appelles = you are called (informal)

activities.prompt: Choose the phrase you hear: “Good morning.”
activities.feedback: Bonjour means good morning / good day. Bonsoir is used in the evening.

activities.prompt: Translate: “My name is Luis.”
activities.hint: Use the fixed pattern Je m'appelle + name.
activities.feedback: Je m'appelle literally means “I call myself,” but the natural translation is “my name is.”

activities.prompt: Which question asks a friend their name?
activities.feedback: The tu form marks the informal/familiar address.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: m'appelle / Je / Sophie
activities.feedback: The fixed chunk is Je m'appelle + name.

activities.prompt: Say a greeting, your name, and Enchanté.
activities.hint: Speak the full three-part introduction aloud.
activities.feedback: A successful introduction contains a greeting, name, and courtesy phrase.

lessons.mission: Introduce yourself to a new contact and close the conversation politely.

dialogue.title: At the registration desk

lines.speaker: A
lines.es: Bonjour, je m'appelle Marta. Comment tu t'appelles ?
lines.en: Hello, my name is Marta. What is your name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.en: My name is Diego. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Nice to meet you. See you later.

learner_turns: Replace Marta and Diego with your own name and a fictional partner.
Repeat the exchange once using formal vous: Comment vous appelez-vous ?

exit_check: Say “Bonjour, je m'appelle …” from memory.
Choose the informal name question (Comment tu t'appelles ?).
Say “Enchanté” and “À plus tard.”

completion_rules.retry_policy: Incorrect essential items return immediately, then again in next-day review.

lessons.title: The Sound System
objectives: pronounce the basic French oral vowels consistently
ask someone to repeat or slow down
use merci and s'il vous plaît in a request

teaching.explanation: French vowel quality differs from English; focus first on clear oral vowels: a as in 'papa', e has several pronunciations, i as in 'si', o as in 'pot', u as in 'tu'. For beginners, prioritize clear vowel sounds and rhythm; perfect accent comes later.
teaching.pattern: Pouvez-vous répéter ? = Can you repeat? Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît. = More slowly, please. Je ne comprends pas. = I do not understand.
teaching.memory_tip: Attach each vowel to a gesture or image and retrieve the sound before looking at the written word.

examples.analysis: pouvez-vous = can you; répéter = to repeat
plus = more; lentement = slowly; s'il vous plaît = please

activities.prompt: Choose the word with the /i/ vowel:
activities.feedback: Oui has the clear /i/ sound.

activities.prompt: Translate: “Please repeat.”
activities.hint: Use the command chunk Répétez plus s'il vous plaît or Pouvez-vous répéter ?
activities.feedback: Répétez is a practical classroom command “repeat.” Pouvez-vous répéter ? is polite.

activities.prompt: You did not understand. What should you say?
activities.feedback: Je ne comprends pas means “I do not understand.”

activities.prompt: Match the repair phrase to its meaning.
activities.answer: Pouvez-vous répéter ? = Can you repeat?; Plus lentement = More slowly; Merci = Thank you.
activities.feedback: These phrases keep a conversation moving even with limited grammar.

activities.prompt: Ask a partner to repeat more slowly and thank them.
activities.answer: Pouvez-vous répéter ? Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît. Merci.
activities.feedback: Use the whole repair sequence aloud.

lessons.mission: Keep a conversation alive when you miss a sound or word.

dialogue.title: Repairing a missed word

lines.speaker: B
lines.es: Je ne comprends pas. Pouvez-vous répéter ?
lines.en: I do not understand. Can you repeat?

learner_turns: Read B aloud without looking at the English.

exit_check: Say all five vowels aloud twice.
Retrieve the phrase for “I do not understand.”
Ask for repetition and slower speech.

lessons.title: People and Pronouns
objectives: recognize the main subject pronouns
use suis and es in short identity sentences
ask and answer where someone is from

teaching.explanation: French normally uses subject pronouns with verbs; beginners should keep pronouns visible while learning conjugation patterns. Vous serves as formal singular and plural; tu is informal singular.
teaching.pattern: Je suis = I am. Tu es = you are. Il/Elle est = he/she is. Nous sommes = we are. Vous êtes = you are (formal or plural).
teaching.contrast: Do not translate English “you are” into a single French form: use tu for familiar singular and vous for formal singular or plural.

examples.analysis: je = I; suis = am; de/du = from/of

activities.prompt: Which word means “I”?
Translate: “I am from Chile.”
activities.feedback: French may use de or du depending on the country name (du for masculine country names). Both Je suis du Chili and Je suis du Chili are acceptable phrasing.

activities.prompt: Choose the informal singular question:
Complete: Elle ___ d'Espagne.
activities.feedback: Elle takes the third-person singular form est.

activities.prompt: Answer in French: D'où es-tu ?
activities.hint: Use a real or invented country/city.
activities.feedback: A complete answer is Je suis de + place.

lessons.mission: Exchange identity information with a new classmate.

lines.speaker: B
lines.es: Je suis de Colombie. Et toi ?
lines.en: I am from Colombia. And you?

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: I am from the United States. Nice to meet you.

exit_check: Identify je, tu, il, elle, nous, and vous.
Say where you are from.
Ask a familiar person where they are from.

completion_rules.retry_policy: Incorrect essential items return immediately, then again in next-day review.

lessons.title: Nouns Have a Profile
objectives: identify common noun gender cues
use le/la and un/une with singular nouns
make regular nouns plural

teaching.explanation: Every French noun has grammatical gender. Many nouns ending in -e are feminine and many others are masculine; this is a useful pattern but has many exceptions. Learn each noun with its article.
teaching.pattern: le livre / les livres; la maison / les maisons; un ami / une amie. Add -s to form most regular plurals; pronunciation may not change.
teaching.warning: Gender is grammatical, not a statement about the real-world object. Exceptions must be learned as vocabulary.

activities.prompt: Choose the correct phrase for “the house”:
Complete: ___ livre (the book).
Translate: “the books”
activities.feedback: Livre ends in a vowel sound and the plural written form adds -s; the plural article is les.

activities.prompt: Classify: maisons
Produce a noun phrase for “a friend” using ami.
activities.hint: Use un with the masculine form or une with the feminine form.
activities.feedback: The article must agree with the noun: un ami or une amie.

lessons.mission: Identify and describe objects in a simple environment.

dialogue.title: Labeling a desk
learner_turns: Point to or imagine three objects and name them with an article.

exit_check: Choose le, la, les, or les for four noun phrases.
Make livre, maison, ami, and carte plural.
Produce one masculine and one feminine noun phrase.

completion_rules.retry_policy: Incorrect essential items return immediately, then again in next-day review.

lessons.title: Describe a Person
objectives: place a basic adjective after a noun when needed
match adjective gender and number in common patterns
say whether someone is a student, friend, or teacher

teaching.explanation: Many French adjectives follow the noun and change for gender and number. Common patterns include grand/grande and adjectives that end in -e which are often identical for both genders (e.g., sympathique, calme).
teaching.pattern: Il/Elle est + adjective = He/She is + adjective. Elle est grande. Il est grand.
teaching.strategy: Learn adjectives in a pair such as grand/grande rather than memorizing only the English gloss.

examples.analysis: elle + est + feminine adjective (sympathique is same form)

activities.prompt: Choose the feminine form:
Translate: “She is friendly.”
activities.feedback: Sympathique ends in -e and is identical for masculine and feminine forms in this case.

activities.prompt: Complete: des amis ___ (friendly).
Correct the sentence: Elle est grand.
activities.feedback: Elle requires the feminine adjective grande in this regular pattern.

activities.prompt: Describe a fictional person with two adjectives.
activities.hint: Choose matching forms such as grand/grande and sympathique.
activities.feedback: Say a complete sentence, not a list of words.

lessons.mission: Give a short description of a person.

dialogue.title: Introducing a colleague

lines.speaker: B
lines.es: C'est mon amie. Elle est sympathique et grande.
lines.en: She is my friend. She is friendly and tall.

lines.speaker: B
lines.es: C'est mon ami. Il est calme.
lines.en: He is my friend. He is calm.

learner_turns: Say the dialogue as both speakers.

exit_check: Match four adjectives to masculine and feminine forms.
Correct one agreement error.
Describe one imaginary person with two adjectives.

lessons.title: Questions and Answers
objectives: ask who, what, where, and how questions
distinguish quoi from qui and où
answer with a complete phrase rather than a single word

teaching.explanation: French question words include quoi, qui, où, comment, quand. Spoken questions often use intonation or the full form Qu'est-ce que c'est ?; written questions do not use inverted punctuation as in Spanish.
teaching.pattern: Qu'est-ce que c'est ? = What is it? Qui est ? = Who is it? Où est ? = Where is it? Comment ça va ? = How are you?
teaching.note: This week, learn question words as retrieval cues. Full verb conjugation for être and other verbs continues in later lessons.

activities.prompt: Which word means “where”?
Translate: “Who is she?”
Match each question word: quoi = what; qui = who; où = where; comment = how.
activities.answer: quoi = what; qui = who; où = where; comment = how.

activities.prompt: Put in order: est / Où / ceci ?
activities.feedback: The natural location question in beginner French can be Où est ceci ?; the exercise accepts common forms and will introduce more natural spoken alternatives later.

activities.prompt: Ask and answer: What is this?
activities.feedback: Use the question and a full noun phrase in the answer.

lessons.mission: Ask for basic information instead of guessing.

dialogue.title: Question drill
learner_turns: Replace carte and amie with your own words.
Ask all four question words aloud.

exit_check: Retrieve quoi, qui, où, and comment.
Ask two questions and answer them with complete phrases.
Use standard written question forms for beginner French.

lessons.title: Week 1 Field Check
objectives: hold a 60–90 second basic introduction
understand a short introduction at slow speed
combine identity, origin, noun phrases, and descriptions

teaching.explanation: Today is a retrieval day. Do not reread the week first. Attempt the checkpoint from memory, then review only the items you miss. The goal is flexible recombination, not reciting one script.
teaching.pattern: Bonjour. Je m'appelle ____. Je suis de ____. Je suis étudiant(e). Mon ami(e) est ____. Enchanté.
teaching.checkpoint: You must greet, give a name and origin, ask one question, describe one person, and repair one misunderstanding.

examples.es: Bonjour, je m'appelle Carlos. Je suis du Pérou.
examples.en: Hello, my name is Carlos. I am from Peru.

activities.prompt: Without hints, write the French for “My name is …” and “I am from …”.
Translate and then say: “Hello. I am from Mexico. Nice to meet you.”
activities.answer: Bonjour. Je suis du Mexique. Enchanté.

activities.prompt: After hearing a short introduction, identify the speaker’s name and country.
activities.feedback: The app should generate or select a slow audio clip using Week 1 vocabulary.

activities.prompt: Correct: Mon amie est sympathique (if necessary).
Complete the field check with a simulated partner.
activities.answer: Bonjour. Je m'appelle ____. Je suis de ____. Comment tu t'appelles ? Enchanté.
activities.feedback: Pass when you complete the exchange, ask one follow-up, and use one repair phrase if needed.

lessons.mission: Complete a first-contact conversation using the entire Week 1 toolkit.

lines.speaker: A
lines.es: Bonjour. Je m'appelle Ana. Je suis du Mexique. Comment tu t'appelles ?
lines.en: Hello. My name is Ana. I am from Mexico. What is your name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.es: Je m'appelle ____. Je suis de ____. Enchanté.
lines.en: My name is ____. I am from ____. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: B
lines.es: C'est mon ami(e). Il/Elle est sympathique.
lines.en: He/she is my friend. He/she is friendly.

learner_turns: Perform the dialogue without looking at the English.

exit_check: Complete the introduction from memory.
Understand the core meaning of a short introduction.
Pass the roleplay with at least 80% accuracy and one spontaneous substitution.
